Production

2026

Beef production is forecast to rise 6 percent in 2026 to 2.3 MMT CWE. The 2026 forecast is tied to the market shifts caused by the NWS trade crisis. The increase does not reflect herd growth, which remains largely flat, but rather a shift from exporting live cattle to processing them domestically. With live exports to the U.S. forecast to fall to zero in 2026 due to NWS-related sanitary restrictions, these animals will now need to be finished and slaughtered within Mexico. Cattle that missed their export window in 2025 have spent additional months on feedlots. These animals are being slaughtered in 2026 at much higher weights than the typical export-ready calf.

2025

Beef production is estimated to decrease 4 percent in 2025 to 2.17 MMT CWE. Although early forecasts had suggested a modest increase, revised 2025 estimates now indicate a decline, reflecting the logistical disruptions caused by the NWS outbreak. The government of Mexico has implemented strict movement controls, making it difficult and expensive to transport cattle from southern breeding grounds to northern feedlots and TIF slaughterhouses. Producers faced new costs for mandatory inspections, immersion baths, and certifications. For many small-to-medium ranchers, these added sanitary cost made it more profitable to hold cattle in anticipation of the U.S. border reopening, rather than sending them to slaughter.

Consumption

2026

Beef consumption is forecast to rise 6 percent in 2026, reaching 2.31 million metric tons CWE. This recovery is driven by a combination of improved domestic supply, a more favorable economic environment, and strong demand from the Hotel, Restaurant, and Institution (HRI) sector. A key factor supporting this increase is the redirection of cattle into the domestic market. Following the suspension of live cattle exports to the U.S. due to the detection of NWS in southern Mexico, ranchers are increasingly finishing these animals in local feedlots. As a result, cattle slaughter is projected to rise in 2026, significantly boosting the domestic availability of beef.

This shift is expected to create a substantial supply-side push. With domestic slaughter increasing and live exports falling to zero, supply is likely to exceed typical domestic demand, putting downward pressure on wholesale beef prices. This dynamic will make beef more competitive compared to the volatile prices and inflationary pressures seen in 2025.

The 2026 outlook is further supported by a more robust consumer base. A 13 percent increase in the minimum wage, effective January 2026, is expected to strengthen the purchasing power of lower- and middle-income households, while macroeconomic conditions remain favorable. The HRI sector continues to be the most dynamic driver of beef demand. Mexico enters 2026 with record-breaking tourism and a strong peso, with international arrivals projected to grow more than six percent year-over-year. This is sustaining demand for high-quality cuts in resorts and urban centers. Meanwhile, rapid expansion of quick-service restaurant (QSR) chains is driving consumption of processed beef products, such as burgers and tacos, reflecting the preferences of Mexico’s urbanizing population.

2025

Beef consumption is estimated to decrease by 1 percent in 2025 to 2.19 MMT CWE. While Mexico’s headline inflation has shown signs of easing, core food inflation remains a significant hurdle. Beef prices have risen at a faster rate than other proteins, leading to reduced purchasing power. High prices for popular cuts, including ground beef, sliced cuts, and loins have forced middle and lower-income households to tighten their budgets.

Historically, oilseed production has offered better profitability compared to grains. Contacts indicated, if the growth in global fuel and fertilizer prices continues well into calendar year (CY) 2026, some farmers might switch from grains to oilseeds. Industry also noted medium and large farmers have already purchased the necessary inputs for spring planting and have prepared their fields for a specific crop. This will limit any significant deviations in perspective plantings for MY2026/27. However, contacts note small farmers are more likely to make their planting decisions later; therefore, Post will make any necessary oilseed adjustments based on CY2026 MEEA planting data.

Post estimates MY2026/27 total oilseed area at 8.6 million hectares (ha), which is equivalent to the five-year average. According to SSSU official data, 1.3 million ha of winter rapeseed has already been planted. This area is 11 percent higher than in MY2025/26. Post accepts this number as the initial estimate for MY2026/27 rapeseed area, as spring rapeseed areas are minimal. The remainder of the total estimated oilseed area will be split between two spring crops: sunflower and soybeans. Imports of sunflower seeds are higher ahead of MY2026/27 planting season compared to the previous MY (Figure 1). Some of these volumes might have been imported for domestic processing to compensate for a shortage of domestic sunflower seeds in MY2025/26; however, there is an increase in imports from destinations that historically supply sunflower seeds for planting. Post uses this as a valid argument to increase its MY2026/27 sunflower area estimate to 5.4 million ha, a 6 percent increase compared to Post’s previous MY estimate.

Based on the total estimated oilseed area, Post forecasts MY2026/27 soybean area at 1.8 million ha, an 11 percent decrease against Post’s previous MY estimate.

At the time of report writing, the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) was close to the long-term average (Figure 2). This indicates there are no significant issues for winter crops, specifically winter rapeseed. Note that NDVI is a standardized measure of vegetation. High values indicate healthier vegetation, while low values indicate low or no vegetation.

Mid-March 2026, the beginning of planting season, featured sufficient amounts of both surface and sub-surface moisture (Figures 3 and 4). This indicates plants will have good conditions immediately after planting and a sufficient amount of moisture after germination.
